### Minimum Acceptable Standard

> Source: Quality Bar §4 — the minimum standard, per dimension (Security / UX Trust / UI-Product Packaging / Performance-Cost), that the outcome above must meet to actually count as delivered. This answers a different question than the outcome itself: not "was it built" but "was it built to a standard that makes it safe/trustworthy/usable/affordable to rely on."
> Fold in only the dimensions the source states are material for this project — skip any the source marks not applicable. Do not invent a standard the source didn't state.
> A dimension deliberately left out of this document (because it is genuinely internal-only and not something an external reader needs) is not simply skipped here — it must be recorded as Omit with a reason in the Fidelity Ledger. The default, when in doubt, is to include it: a minimum standard a project promises to meet is normally something the reader is entitled to know.

## Scope

> Source: Scope Boundary §6 (in scope / out of scope / non-goals), plus:
> — any constraint from §7 marked non-negotiable that functions as a real boundary (example: a required or forbidden platform) rather than a pure implementation preference;
> — any Functional Requirement from §9 tagged **Sovereign** that materially changes what the project promises to deliver (example: "must let the user export the final report") and is not already covered by Goals above. A Sovereign requirement is the Director's actual destination, not a current best guess — it does not get to disappear here. A requirement tagged **Operationalization** is ARC's present translation of that destination and defaults to Omit unless it is independently risk-relevant.
> Class: Preserve. A forbidden option stays forbidden in the output — do not soften it into a neutral-sounding preference.
